summary =1

Question 82. A complete data-summary audit

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original integrated examination problem

A report claims: “Eight values have mean 5, descriptive variance 4, corrected variance 4, and RMS 3. After adding 10 to every value, SD increases by 10 and correlation with another unchanged column increases.” Identify every mathematically forced defect, and state what cannot be concluded about the correlation.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

For n=8 and v=4, corrected variance must be 8·4/7=32/7, not 4. RMS squared must be v+x¯2=4+25=29, so RMS is 29, not 3. Translation changes mean to 15 but leaves centered deviations, variance, and SD unchanged; descriptive SD remains 2. If both paired columns are nonconstant, translation leaves correlation unchanged. If the other column is constant, correlation is undefined and no increase can be claimed. These checks require no reconstruction of all eight values and expose both denominator and invariance errors.

20. Examination rules and advanced pitfalls

Read these complete rules after the lesson. Each states an actionable condition, consequence, or counterexample; none replaces the derivation above.

Complete examination rules and final conceptual checks

Use these rules after reading the derivations. Each rule states its contract; a shortcut without its assumptions is not a valid solution.

Rule 1

Identify the observational unit before averaging. A student-weighted mean and an equally weighted mean of class means answer different questions when class sizes differ.

Rule 2

A numerical category code is not automatically a numerical measurement. Arbitrary recoding preserves category frequencies but can change its arithmetic mean completely.

Rule 3

Ordinal ordering permits rank comparisons but does not justify equal spacing between categories. A difference between adjacent codes need not represent equal scientific change.

Rule 4

Missing values are not zeros. Mean imputation leaves the observed mean unchanged while reducing the computed residual spread, so it must not be treated as neutral evidence.

Rule 5

Repeated measurements and duplicated rows are still separate recorded entries for descriptive arithmetic. They are not automatically independent observations for inference.

Rule 6

A frequency table of exact distinct values preserves the multiset but loses order. An interval frequency table additionally loses positions inside the intervals.

Rule 7

A density histogram's bin height is fj/(nwj), where wj>0 is the bin width. Its area, not its height, is the bin's empirical mass.

Rule 8

Unequal-width bins with equal counts must have different density heights. Comparing raw heights as if they were counts can reverse the visual conclusion.

Rule 9

State a nonoverlapping bin endpoint convention. In this chapter bins are left-closed and right-open, except that the last bin includes its final right endpoint.

Rule 10

Histogram mass is normalized by ∑jhjwj=1. Summing heights alone is generally meaningless unless all widths are one in the chosen units.

Rule 11

An exact unweighted histogram also requires integer counts nhjwj. A normalized density with fractional implied counts is a model, not necessarily the exact display of the stated finite list.

Rule 12

Within-bin interpolation assumes a distribution of mass inside a bin. Counts alone cannot determine the exact fraction in a strict subinterval of that bin.

Rule 13

Bin boundaries can hide or create apparent modes. Check the observations or ECDF before concluding that a visible bump identifies a distinct population.

Rule 14

Sturges and Freedman–Diaconis are binning heuristics, not coverage theorems. A zero IQR can make the latter width degenerate despite a real extreme tail.

Rule 15

The ECDF is Fn(t)=n−1#{i:xi≤t}. Its value includes all observations equal to the threshold, while its left limit excludes them.

Rule 16

The jump at a value is its empirical frequency. Tied records form one jump of multiplicity divided by sample size, not several separated value locations.

Rule 17

The interval (a,b] has mass Fn(b)−Fn(a). The interval [a,b] instead has mass Fn(b)−Fn(a−); changing a bracket matters when endpoints are observed.

Rule 18

The interval [a,b) has mass Fn(b−)−Fn(a−). In a discrete empirical distribution, continuous-population habits of ignoring endpoint mass are unsafe.

Rule 19

An ECDF determines relative multiplicities, but not the sample size when the entire multiset may have been duplicated. It also cannot recover time order or paired-column identities.

Rule 20

The mean preserves the total: ∑ixi=nx¯. For group means, multiply each mean by its group size before combining totals.

Rule 21

The mean uniquely minimizes squared loss on a nonempty list. The identity ∑i(xi−c)2=M2+n(c−x¯)2 proves this without calculus.

Rule 22

The weighted mean minimizes weighted squared loss when weights are nonnegative and their total is positive. Negative weights invalidate the ordinary mass and minimization interpretation.

Rule 23

The mean of ratios is not generally the ratio of totals. For overall speed, derive total distance divided by total time before selecting arithmetic or harmonic averaging.

Rule 24

Equal-distance speeds use a harmonic mean, while equal-time speeds use an arithmetic mean. The exposure contract determines the appropriate weighting.

Rule 25

Multiplicative growth uses positive factors and their geometric mean. Averaging signed percentage changes does not preserve the compounded product.

Rule 26

The midpoint median uses one middle record for odd size and the mean of two middle records for even size. It is a selected convention, not a universally shared definition of every 50th percentile.

Rule 27

Every center between the two middle records minimizes absolute loss for even size. The midpoint is one minimizer; uniqueness fails when those records differ.

Rule 28

A weighted absolute-loss minimizer has no more than half the total weight strictly on either side. A lower weighted median is the first value whose cumulative weight reaches half.

Rule 29

A mode maximizes frequency and minimizes categorical mismatch loss. The mode can be absent as a unique choice when several values tie for the largest count.

Rule 30

For nearest-rank quantiles with 0<p≤1, use sorted position ⌈np⌉. At p=0, the chapter explicitly uses the minimum; blindly using index zero would be invalid.

Rule 31

Type-7 quantiles use h=1+(n−1)p and interpolate the surrounding order statistics. They can return a value never observed in the data.

Rule 32

Median-of-halves, nearest rank and type 7 can produce different quartiles on the same list. State the chosen convention before computing IQR, fences or a boxplot.

Rule 33

Increasing affine transformations preserve the order and commute with the stated quantile calculations. Decreasing transformations reverse ranks and require checking how each quantile convention treats the endpoints.

Rule 34

Midpoint medians commute with negative affine scaling. A lower nearest-rank median need not: for an even list it selects a different original middle record after reversal.

Rule 35

A quantile level is not a promise that exactly that percentage of finite records lies strictly below the returned value. Ties and finite rank increments prevent such an equality in general.

Rule 36

The centered sum M2=∑i(xi−x¯)2 is nonnegative. It vanishes exactly when every observation equals the same value.

Rule 37

Descriptive variance is v=M2/n for n≥1. Corrected sample variance is s2=M2/(n−1) only for n>1; a singleton's corrected variance is undefined rather than zero.

Rule 38

For a nonconstant list with n>1, s2=nv/(n−1)>v. If both are zero, cancelling them to infer sample size is invalid.

Rule 39

Raw totals give M2=∑ixi2−(∑ixi)2/n. Before normalizing, check that these totals satisfy Cauchy–Schwarz and produce no negative centered sum.

Rule 40

RMS measures distance from zero, not spread about the mean. Its exact relation is RMS2=v+x¯2.

Rule 41

Under iid finite-variance sampling, E[M2]=(n−1)σ2. Independence makes Var(X¯)=σ2/n; normality is not needed for this expectation calculation.

Rule 42

Bessel correction does not repair arbitrary dependence or selection bias. Identical dependent readings can have zero sample spread even when their common random value has positive population variance.

Rule 43

Unbiased variance does not imply unbiased SD. Concavity of square root generally lowers E[s] below σ, and reciprocals require separate positivity and integrability checks.

Rule 44

Frequency weights represent repeated records and use correction denominator W−1. Deterministic weights on independent equal-variance observations use W−W2/W, where W2=∑iwi2; the meanings cannot be interchanged.

Rule 45

The effective size W2/W2 describes the variance of a weighted mean under its sampling assumptions. It is neither the total weight nor a literal fractional count of people.

Rule 46

Translation changes the mean but leaves centered sums, variances, SD and IQR unchanged. An argument that SD rises by an added constant confuses origin with spread.

Rule 47

Under Y=aX+b, variance scales by a2 and SD by |a|. A negative standard deviation is always an invalid result.

Rule 48

With descriptive standardization, score sum is zero and squared-score sum is n. With corrected standardization, squared-score sum is n−1; identify which score variance is one.

Rule 49

Standardization changes location and scale but does not make a distribution normal. Normal probabilities require a separate justified or explicitly supplied model.

Rule 50

CV is meaningful only with an appropriate nonzero reference mean and ratio-scale interpretation. It is invariant under positive unit scaling but changes under translation.

Rule 51

A boxplot fence is a threshold calculated from quartiles. A whisker ends at the furthest retained observed value, which need not equal that threshold.

Rule 52

Under the chapter's strict outlier rule, a value exactly on a fence is retained. If the upper fence itself is observed, it is necessarily the upper whisker.

Rule 53

A labelled boxplot outlier is a statistical flag, not proof of recording error. Deleting it requires evidence about data collection and the intended analysis.

Rule 54

Zero IQR or raw MAD does not imply zero variance. A heavily tied center with a single extreme observation provides a direct counterexample.

Rule 55

Median absolute deviation uses a median of absolute residuals about a median. Mean absolute deviation uses an average and a specified center; neither name should replace its actual definition.

Rule 56

Trimming removes records; Winsorization replaces extremes and retains the size. State the count changed at each end and recompute the resulting denominator.

Rule 57

Robustness does not mean exact invariance under every replacement. A changed middle record can alter the median even though sending a maximum farther away does not change that same median.

Rule 58

Reflection symmetry implies equal reflected frequencies, not merely an equal mean and median. Equal centers or zero third central moment provide too few constraints to prove symmetry.

Rule 59

Moment skewness requires m2>0 and is m3/m23/2. Under negative scaling it changes sign; under translation it does not change.

Rule 60

Moment kurtosis is m4/m22, and excess subtracts 3. State this convention because some software uses bias-corrected variants and some informal sources reverse the excess sign.

Rule 61

Cauchy–Schwarz gives moment kurtosis at least one. Equality for an unweighted nonconstant list requires equal-magnitude positive and negative residuals with equal counts.

Rule 62

The heuristic mode≈3median−2mean is not an identity. Multimodal or irregular finite lists can violate familiar verbal skewness orderings.

Rule 63

For nonnegative data, at most nx¯/t observations can be at least t>0. Negative observations invalidate this finite Markov argument by allowing compensation in the total.

Rule 64

For centered spread, a tail record at distance at least t costs at least t2 of M2. Therefore its count is at most M2/t2, with integer rounding and the correct variance denominator applied afterward.

Rule 65

A strict tail costs strictly more than t2 per record. When the squared-energy ratio is an integer, the strict bound loses one compared with the closed bound; otherwise its floor may stay the same.

Rule 66

An upper bound is not automatically attainable. An extremal construction must satisfy both the prescribed squared-deviation sum and the zero signed-deviation sum.

Rule 67

A single centered residual satisfies |di|≤(n−1)v. The other residuals must sum to its negative, and that constraint sharpens the simpler bound obtained from its own square alone.

Rule 68

For values in [a,b], v≤(b−x¯)(x¯−a)≤(b−a)2/4. A known mean can sharpen the unconditional range bound.

Rule 69

Equal-weight finite records impose integer endpoint masses. The exact unconstrained maximum range variance is (b−a)2⌊n2/4⌋/n2, so odd size cannot attain the continuous half-and-half bound.

Rule 70

The normal 68–95–99.7 percentages concern a normal population. They are neither a theorem for arbitrary lists nor exact required frequencies in each sample from a normal population.

Rule 71

Midpoint group summaries describe a replaced list. They need not equal, consistently understate or consistently overstate the true raw variance; interval counts omit within-bin locations.

Rule 72

The midpoint mean error is at most the frequency-weighted average half-width. Endpoint inclusion determines whether the corresponding upper and lower limits are attained or only approached.

Rule 73

A histogram-interpolated quantile assumes constant density within its containing interval. It does not recover the exact middle records used by a raw midpoint median.

Rule 74

Combined M2 equals within-group M2 plus the weighted squared distances of group means from the combined mean. Averaging group variances without the between term discards real variation.

Rule 75

A pooled within-group estimator uses within sum and denominator N−G under its model. Total descriptive variance instead includes between sum and divides by N; these quantities target different spreads.

Rule 76

Simpson reversal follows from comparing different mixture weights. Group-specific superiority can reverse in the aggregate, and neither comparison alone proves a causal effect.

Rule 77

Welford appending uses the old residual and new mean: M2'=M2+δ(x−x¯'). Appending at the mean leaves M2 unchanged but decreases descriptive variance by increasing the count.

Rule 78

Correlation requires both columns to vary and preserves their original pairing. Zero correlation can coexist with a deterministic curve; a nonzero empirical correlation also does not logically disprove independence of the underlying population.

Rule 79

Pearson measures standardized linear association, Spearman uses average ranks with ties, and tie-free Kendall counts concordant minus discordant pairs. Independently sorting columns destroys record-level association, whereas Q–Q sorting intentionally compares distributions.

Rule 80

A trailing average uses an explicit startup denominator; a centered average requires future data. In EWMA forecasting, the previous summary predicts the next observation, while using the updated summary leaks the target into its own prediction.

21. Editable visual laboratories

The laboratories compute the actual states for your supplied data. They start paused and support step, back, seek, restart, speed, and reduced-motion display. A histogram model uses its declared endpoint rule; a quantile or box model states type 7 versus nearest rank. Finite displayed cases illustrate proofs and do not replace them. Print includes checkpoints and their explanations.

Enter 1–12 finite values per list between −999 and 999. Histogram mode needs strictly increasing edges covering every observation. Pooling and Q–Q accept unequal group sizes; correlation needs equal lengths and labels constant-column correlation undefined. Affine mode uses the numeric scale (−20 to 20) and exactly one translation in the second field. Moving average uses integer window 1–12 and shorter windows at startup. EWMA uses lambda greater than zero and at most one, with initial value zero. Other modes ignore unused fields. Boxplots use type 7 and strict 1.5-IQR fences. Invalid submissions preserve the previous model. The displayed arithmetic uses finite precision; exact rational examples are checked separately.
